title: Rav Acha son of Rav Avya
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Hyman describes him as like a student-colleague of Rav Ashi who took a large part with Rav Ashi in arranging the Talmud, as Hyman says we always find “Rav Acha son of Rav Avya said to Rav Ashi,” as in Eruvin 48b, Pesachim 44b, Ketubot 76a, Nedarim 35a and 51b, Nazir 37a, Gittin 62b (Hyman proposes this reading in Bava Kamma 62a), Bava Metzia 96a, Bava Batra 3a, 46b, 68a, 82a and 103a, and Chullin 17b, 39b and 80a. In all of them he converses with Rav Ashi, Ravina’s colleague (in Hyman’s view, not with an earlier Rav Ashi, whom he rejects as nonexistent). In Bava Metzia 104b he sent before Rav Ashi; and in Eruvin 11b he found Rav Ashi’s students and said to them, “Did the Master say anything about the form of a doorway?” etc.

In Bava Metzia 8a, “Rav Acha son of Rav Ada said to Rav Ashi,” Hyman proposes son of Rav Avya, according to Dikdukei Soferim; and in Chullin 31a, where he asked Rav Menashe, “A needle — what?” Hyman proposes “Rav Ashi,” according to Dikdukei Soferim, for Rav Menashe lived in Rabbah’s time. In Menachot 37a, “Rabbi Chiyya and Rav Acha son of Rav Avya positioned and put on [the tefillin]” — the words “Rabbi Chiyya” are reported by Hyman as deleted in Dikdukei Soferim.

Hyman concludes from all these places that it is clear that he belonged to the generation of Rav Ashi. But Rav Acha bar Avya is a different Amora, a native of the Land of Israel, as explained in his entry; Hyman criticizes Seder HaDorot for confusing them together and for not noticing that Yuchasin too separated them.

notes.text: Saved Davidson Chullin31a paragraphs8–10 explicitly retains Rav Menashe and a needle used for slaughter; Hyman proposes Rav Ashi from Dikdukei Soferim, without overriding that witness. His Menachot37a locator is preserved; the corresponding passage is in saved Davidson37b paragraph3, Rabbi Chiyya and RAV Acha positioning tefillin opposite the heart. His deletion proposal remains attributed, not adopted as the Gemara’s only reading.

The consulted Menachot 37b, rather than supplied 37a, names Rabbi Chiyya and Rav Acha son of Rav Avya positioning tefillin opposite the heart. Hyman’s Dikdukei Soferim deletion remains a reported proposal. His account of Talmud arrangement, rejection of an earlier Rav Ashi and separation from the Palestinian namesake remain his arguments.
